lessons.title: Natural resources: what are they and who uses them?
objectives: Define natural resource and give examples of renewable and non-renewable resources
Explain why some resources are described as finite
Describe how resource use differs between countries

keywords.def: something from nature that people use, such as water, soil, timber or oil
a resource that can be replaced naturally within a human lifetime
a resource that will run out because it takes millions of years to form
limited in amount, so it can be used up
the amount of a resource that is used

starter: Say Bismillah. Name three things you used today that came from nature.
What is the water cycle?
What is the difference between a physical feature and a human feature?

teach.heading: What are natural resources?
bullets: Resources are materials from nature that we use.
Examples: water, soil, wood, metals, oil, coal, wind and sun.
We use resources for food, shelter, energy and goods.
teach.note: Hold up everyday items (a phone, a paper cup, a cotton T-shirt) and ask pupils to trace each back to natural resources. Show how metals in a phone come from mines, plastic comes from oil and cotton comes from plants. Emphasise that all human life depends on resources.

teach.heading: Renewable and non-renewable
bullets: Renewable: sun, wind, water, wood if replanted.
Non-renewable resources took millions of years to form.
teach.note: Misconception: renewable does not mean unlimited in every case. Trees can be cut faster than they grow and then they are not renewable in practice. Pupils should also understand that 'non-renewable' means 'will run out on human timescales'. Ask for examples that are tricky, such as fish or soil.

teach.heading: Unequal use of resources
bullets: Rich countries use far more resources per person.
A person in the USA uses much more energy than a person in India.
Many people still lack safe water, food or electricity.
teach.note: Show a bar graph of energy use per person. High-income countries use many times more. The differences matter because resource use and development are linked. Ask: is it fair? Introduce the idea of a global responsibility to share resources and avoid waste.

teach.heading: Our duty as khalifah
bullets: Muslims believe humans are khalifah on Earth (Qur'an 2:30).
Allah does not love those who waste (Qur'an 7:31).
We take what we need and protect the rest.
teach.note: Link the unit to the Islamic ethos of stewardship (khalifah) and avoiding israf (extravagance). Surah al-Baqarah 2:30 mentions the khalifah and 7:31 says 'eat and drink but do not be wasteful'. Ask pupils how a Muslim should think about using water, electricity and food.

practice: Sort these into renewable or non-renewable: coal, wind, gas, solar, timber, iron ore, fish.
Explain why oil is described as a finite resource.
independent: Create a mind map of five natural resources, their uses and whether they are renewable.
Write a paragraph comparing resource use in a high-income and a low-income country.
Stretch: explain why the line between renewable and non-renewable is not always clear.
exit: Give one example of a resource that can be renewable if managed well.
lessons.homework: Make a list of ten things in your home and write the natural resource each came from.
lessons.send: Provide a card-sort activity with pictures. EAL: key word glossary. Stretch: investigate how recycling changes the idea of finite resources.

lessons.title: Fossil fuels: coal, oil and gas
objectives: Explain how fossil fuels formed
Describe how fossil fuels are used to meet energy needs
Evaluate the advantages and disadvantages of fossil fuels

keywords.def: a fuel formed from the remains of ancient plants and animals, such as coal, oil and gas
a greenhouse gas released when fossil fuels are burned
the trapping of heat in the atmosphere by gases such as carbon dioxide
taking a resource out of the ground
having a reliable and affordable supply of energy

starter: Say Bismillah. What does non-renewable mean?
Give two examples of finite resources.
Why is it unfair that some countries use more resources than others?

teach.heading: How fossil fuels formed
bullets: Coal formed from swamp plants about 300 million years ago.
Oil and gas formed from tiny sea organisms.
Heat and pressure over millions of years changed them.
teach.note: Show a simple diagram. Dead plants or marine plankton were buried under layers of mud and sediment. Over millions of years heat and pressure turned them into coal, oil or gas. Ask: why can we not make more in our lifetime? Because it takes millions of years.

teach.heading: Uses of fossil fuels
bullets: Coal and gas make electricity in power stations.
Oil becomes petrol, diesel and plastics.
Fossil fuels supply about 80% of the world's energy.
teach.note: Show a pie chart of global energy: oil about 30%, coal about 27%, gas about 23%, with the remainder coming from nuclear, hydro and other renewables. Emphasise that many daily goods rely on oil products, not just fuel: plastics, medicines and fertilisers.

teach.heading: Advantages
bullets: They give a lot of energy in a small amount.
They create jobs in extraction and transport.
teach.note: Be balanced. Fossil fuels powered industrial development and lifted many people out of poverty. Gas and oil can be stored and burned on demand, unlike wind and solar which depend on the weather. Ask pupils why fossil fuels are still so widely used.

teach.heading: Disadvantages
bullets: Burning releases carbon dioxide and causes global warming.
Oil spills and mining damage ecosystems.
They will run out and cause conflicts over supply.
teach.note: Link to climate change: carbon dioxide traps heat, a process called the enhanced greenhouse effect. Mention air pollution in cities. Discuss oil spills and mining as local environmental problems. Ask: how could countries without fossil fuels get energy security?

practice: Sequence the stages of coal formation using pictures.
Complete a table: advantages and disadvantages of fossil fuels.
independent: Write an explanation of how oil formed (4 steps).
Evaluate: 'Fossil fuels are still needed today.' Give two points for and two against.
Stretch: explain why countries with large oil reserves may rely too heavily on oil money.
exit: State one environmental problem caused by burning fossil fuels.
lessons.homework: Find out which fossil fuel is most used in your family's home country for electricity and write two facts.
lessons.send: Provide a formation sequence for sorting. EAL: pre-teach carbon dioxide and greenhouse effect with a labelled picture. Stretch: compare carbon emissions of coal and gas.

lessons.title: The energy mix: UK electricity and the world
objectives: Explain what an energy mix is
Describe changes in the UK's electricity mix
Compare the energy mix of different countries

keywords.def: the different sources used to supply a country's energy
energy released by splitting atoms in a reactor
energy sources that do not run out, such as wind and solar
when households cannot afford to heat their homes
reducing the carbon dioxide produced by energy use

starter: Say Bismillah. Name two advantages of fossil fuels.
Name one disadvantage of burning coal.
Which gas is mainly responsible for global warming?

teach.heading: What is an energy mix?
bullets: No country relies on a single energy source.
The mix includes coal, oil, gas, nuclear and renewables.
Each country's mix depends on resources and choices.
teach.note: Show a pie chart from the UK. Ask pupils to estimate each slice. Explain that the mix changes over time due to costs, technology, politics and climate goals. Define electricity versus total energy: electricity is only one part of energy use (transport and heating also matter).

teach.heading: The UK electricity mix
bullets: In 1990, coal produced about two thirds of UK electricity.
In 2023 about 40% came from renewables, mostly wind.
The last UK coal power station closed in September 2024.
teach.note: Show a stacked graph from 1990 to 2023. Gas is still about one third, nuclear about 14%. Ask: what changes do you see? Coal collapsed, wind and solar rose. Reasons: government targets, falling cost of renewables, carbon taxes, air pollution rules. Explain the 'about' in the figures.

teach.heading: Different countries, different mixes
bullets: Iceland uses geothermal and hydro for almost all its electricity.
France gets about two thirds of its electricity from nuclear.
Saudi Arabia and Egypt rely mainly on oil and gas.
teach.note: Link to resources: Iceland has volcanoes and rivers; France chose nuclear after the 1970s oil crisis; Gulf countries have huge oil and gas supplies. Egypt also has big solar projects such as Benban near Aswan (about 1.6 GW). Ask: why do countries choose different mixes?

teach.heading: Challenges of change
bullets: Renewables depend on weather and need storage.
New power lines and wind farms can be costly.
Changing the mix takes years and large investment.
teach.note: Discuss intermittency (wind does not always blow). Batteries and gas backup help. Fuel poverty arises when prices rise and households cannot afford heating: a social problem. Encourage pupils to say what is more important: cost, reliability or lowering carbon.

practice: Describe the changes in UK electricity generation between 1990 and 2023.
Compare the energy mix of two countries using a pie chart.
independent: Draw a pie chart of the UK electricity mix using the data table and write two comments.
Write a paragraph explaining why different countries have different energy mixes.
Stretch: evaluate the claim that nuclear power is the best way to cut carbon emissions.
exit: Which fuel has declined most in the UK electricity mix?
lessons.homework: Find the energy mix of one other country and present it as a simple chart.
lessons.send: Provide a pre-drawn pie chart with sections to complete. EAL: bilingual glossary for energy terms. Stretch: calculate percentage changes from data.

lessons.title: Renewable energy: wind, solar, hydro, geothermal and tidal
objectives: Describe how five renewable energy sources work
Give advantages and disadvantages of each
Match renewable sources to suitable locations

keywords.def: a machine with blades that spins to generate electricity
a device that turns sunlight directly into electricity
electricity made by flowing water turning turbines
heat from inside the Earth used to make electricity or heat buildings
not constant; available only some of the time

starter: Say Bismillah. Define energy mix.
Which fuel's use has fallen most in UK electricity?
Name two renewable sources of energy.

teach.heading: Wind and solar
bullets: Wind turbines turn the wind's movement into electricity.
Solar PV panels turn sunlight into electricity.
Both produce no carbon dioxide when generating.
teach.note: Show photographs of an offshore wind farm and a solar park. Offshore wind farms are bigger and steadier but cost more. Egypt's Benban Solar Park in the desert near Aswan is among the world's largest. Ask pupils what makes a good place for wind (windy, coastal, hills) and for solar (sunny, open, flat).

teach.heading: Water power: hydro and tidal
bullets: Dams store water and release it through turbines (HEP).
Tidal barrages use the rise and fall of the tide.
Dams can flood land and displace people.
teach.note: Explain that HEP is reliable but needs hills and rain; building a dam changes rivers, affects fish and can flood villages. The Aswan High Dam on the Nile is a well-known example in Egypt, with benefits (electricity, flood control) and costs (loss of silt, relocation of communities). Tidal power is predictable but costly.

teach.heading: Geothermal energy
bullets: Heat from underground can make steam for turbines.
Works best near plate boundaries and hot spots.
Iceland heats about nine in ten homes this way.
teach.note: Link back to earlier work on plate boundaries: Iceland sits on the boundary between two plates, so hot rock is close to the surface and living near volcanoes brings benefits such as geothermal energy. Ask why Iceland is ideal and the UK is not.

teach.heading: Biomass and others
bullets: Biomass burns plants or waste for energy.
It can be carbon neutral if replanted.
teach.note: Include a quick note on biomass such as wood pellets, or biogas from farm waste. Misconception: renewable does not automatically mean zero impact. Ask pupils to think about land use, habitats and transport emissions when assessing biomass.

practice: Complete a table: source | how it works | advantage | disadvantage.
Match five locations to the best renewable source: Sahara, Iceland, Scottish coast, Norwegian mountains, Bristol Channel.
independent: Create an information leaflet for one renewable source.
Write a paragraph explaining why no single renewable source suits every country.
Stretch: evaluate hydroelectric power using social, economic and environmental points.
exit: State how a wind turbine produces electricity.
Give one disadvantage of renewable energy.
lessons.homework: Research a renewable energy project in the Middle East or Africa and write three facts.
lessons.send: Provide a labelled diagram for each source. EAL: picture cards. Stretch: include costs per kWh or capacity factors in evaluation.

lessons.title: Decision making: which energy source should Marsa choose?
objectives: Compare energy sources using criteria
Make and justify a decision using evidence
Recognise that different stakeholders prefer different options

keywords.def: standards used to compare or judge options
a person or group affected by a decision
giving up some of one thing to gain another
give reasons or evidence to support a decision

starter: Say Bismillah. Name two renewable energy sources.
Why is solar energy intermittent?
Give an example of a place where geothermal energy is used.

teach.heading: The scenario
bullets: Marsa is a fictional island nation.
It has sun, wind and a small amount of gas.
It needs 500 MW of new electricity.
teach.note: Explain that this is an invented scenario created for practice. Marsa is a hot, windy island of 2 million people with a growing economy. Pupils will act as advisers to the government. Introduce the three options on the next slide.

teach.heading: The options
bullets: Option A: a gas power station.
Option B: a large offshore wind farm.
Option C: a solar park with batteries.
teach.note: Give each option fictional but realistic characteristics: A is cheap to build and reliable but emits carbon dioxide and relies on imported gas; B has no fuel cost and provides jobs but may harm seabirds and takes years; C uses the strong sun, is quiet and clean but requires land and expensive batteries.

teach.heading: Judging the options
bullets: Use criteria: cost, reliability, pollution, jobs.
Think about who gains and who loses.
teach.note: Model one row of the matrix on the board. Ask: is a lower score for cost more important than a higher score for pollution? Different stakeholders (fishermen, hotel owners, government, young people) may weight criteria differently. Encourage pupils to say 'it depends on...'.

teach.heading: Writing a justified recommendation
teach.note: Provide this frame: 'I recommend Option ___ because ___. Another reason is ___. However, ___. This can be reduced by ___.' Reminder: marks in GCSE geography decision-making questions reward a clear decision supported by evidence and an awareness of other views.

practice: In groups, score each option on the decision matrix and total the scores.
Discuss which stakeholder would object most to your choice and why.
independent: Write a 150-word recommendation to the government of Marsa.
Add a table of advantages and disadvantages for your chosen option.
Stretch: propose a combination of two options and justify it.
exit: State your recommendation in one sentence.
lessons.homework: Interview someone at home: which energy source would they choose for a new power plant and why? Write a summary.
lessons.send: Provide the sentence frame and a partially completed matrix. EAL: use icons for criteria. Stretch: weight criteria and recalculate the scores.

lessons.title: Water resources: supply, demand and stress
objectives: Describe the distribution of water on Earth and in different countries
Explain what water stress means and why it happens
Evaluate ways to manage water supply using Egypt and the Nile as an example

keywords.def: water with very little salt, suitable for drinking and farming
when demand for water is higher than the supply available
reliable access to enough safe water
supplying land with water to grow crops
removing salt from sea water to make it drinkable

starter: Say Bismillah. Name the stages of the water cycle.
Why is water called a renewable resource?
Name a country with a desert climate.

teach.heading: Water on Earth
bullets: About 97.5% of water is salty. Only 2.5% is fresh.
Most fresh water is frozen in ice caps and glaciers.
Less than 1% of fresh water is easy to reach.
teach.note: Show a bar or pie chart or use a bucket demonstration: 100 litres of water for the planet, only 2.5 litres is fresh and only a teaspoon is available in rivers and lakes. Ask pupils how this changes the way they think about water. Link to Qur'an 21:30.

teach.heading: Where is water short?
bullets: Water stress affects hot, dry or crowded regions.
Over 2 billion people lack safe drinking water.
Demand rises with population, farming and industry.
teach.note: Show a map of water stress: the Middle East, North Africa and parts of South Asia are highest. Explain that water stress occurs when a country has less than about 1,700 cubic metres per person per year, and scarcity below 1,000. Egypt has under 600.

teach.heading: Egypt and the Nile
bullets: About 97% of Egypt's water comes from the Nile.
Most Egyptians live along the Nile Valley and Delta.
Farming uses most of the water.
teach.note: Show a satellite image: a green ribbon of life through the desert. The Nile is shared by 11 countries, which can cause tension. Egypt has the Aswan High Dam for storage and electricity. Ask: why would a country upstream building a dam concern Egypt? Keep the discussion balanced and respectful.

teach.heading: Managing water supply
bullets: Desalination turns sea water into fresh water.
Efficient irrigation, recycling and repairing leaks save water.
teach.note: Compare strategies on cost, energy use and sustainability. Desalination is common in the Gulf but energy-intensive. Drip irrigation saves water compared with flooding fields. Islam discourages waste in everything we use (Qur'an 7:31); link this to modern water saving at home, such as shorter showers and taking care with wudu.

practice: Calculate the percentage of fresh water that is easily accessible, using the data.
Match each water management strategy with an advantage and a disadvantage.
independent: Write a case study summary of water in Egypt: cause of stress, effects, solutions.
Draw an annotated sketch of a river basin showing a dam, reservoir and irrigation.
Stretch: evaluate which solution is best for a poor country and justify your answer.
exit: Name two ways to increase water supply.
lessons.homework: Record how many litres of water your household uses in one day for washing and drinking and suggest two savings.
lessons.send: Provide a data table and simplified graph. EAL: key terms with pictures. Stretch: compare water use in Egypt and the UK per person.

lessons.title: Food resources and food security
objectives: Define food security and food insecurity
Explain the causes of hunger in some parts of the world
Evaluate strategies to increase food supply and reduce waste

keywords.def: everyone always having enough safe and nutritious food
not getting enough of the right food to stay healthy
an extreme shortage of food across a large area
the distance food travels from where it is grown to where it is eaten
edible food that is thrown away

starter: Say Bismillah. Define water stress.
Name two causes of water shortage.
Where does your family's food come from? Name a food that travels a long way.

teach.heading: What is food security?
bullets: Food security is having enough food at all times.
Food insecurity means people may go hungry.
More than 700 million people face hunger today.
teach.note: Show a global hunger map. About 1 in 11 people worldwide faced hunger in 2023, but in Africa it is closer to 1 in 5. Distinguish between hunger (not enough calories) and malnutrition (lack of balanced diet). Be sensitive: some pupils may have family experience of food shortages.

teach.heading: Why do people go hungry?
bullets: Conflict and disasters destroy crops and supplies.
Climate change causes drought and floods.
teach.note: Hunger is more often caused by poverty, conflict and access than by a lack of food overall: the world produces enough food, but it is unevenly distributed. Use drought and conflict in the Horn of Africa as an example, and handle it sensitively as some pupils may have family links to affected regions.

teach.heading: Increasing food supply
bullets: Irrigation and better seeds raise yields.
Fertilisers and machines help but can harm the environment.
Technology like drip irrigation and greenhouses saves water.
teach.note: Discuss the Green Revolution: improved wheat and rice varieties increased yields from the 1960s, especially in India. The costs included heavy use of chemicals and water. Compare intensive farming with organic or small-scale farming. Ask pupils to evaluate each approach.

teach.heading: Wasting less
bullets: About one third of food produced is lost or wasted.
Plan meals, store food well and share with others.
Islam teaches us not to waste food and to feed the hungry.
teach.note: Link to Islamic ethos: Muslims are encouraged to share food and avoid israf, extravagance (Qur'an 7:31). Charity such as sadaqah and zakat helps people in need. Ask: what practical steps can your family take to waste less, particularly around Ramadan and Eid?

practice: Make a cause-and-effect diagram showing three causes of food insecurity.
Rank four strategies (irrigation, GM crops, reducing waste, trade) from most to least effective and justify.
independent: Write a paragraph explaining why some countries experience food shortages.
Design a poster to reduce food waste at home with five tips.
Stretch: evaluate whether technology alone can solve world hunger.
exit: Give one cause of hunger and one solution.
lessons.homework: Keep a food waste diary for two days and write one action to reduce it.
lessons.send: Provide a flow chart template. EAL: pre-teach cause/effect vocabulary. Stretch: compare strategies to reduce hunger in a named country.

lessons.title: Sustainable living: carbon footprints and unit assessment
objectives: Explain what a carbon footprint is and how to reduce it
Describe what sustainable development means
Complete an end-of-unit assessment on resources

keywords.def: the total greenhouse gases produced by a person, product or activity
development that meets today's needs without harming future generations
ways of cutting waste and saving resources
turning waste into new products

starter: Say Bismillah. Define food security.
Name two renewable energy sources.
Why is a country's energy mix important?

teach.heading: Our carbon footprint
bullets: A carbon footprint measures greenhouse gas emissions.
The average UK person emits about 5 tonnes of CO2 a year.
The USA is about 14 tonnes. India is about 2 tonnes.
teach.note: Use figures rounded: they vary by year and source. Show a graph. Ask why the footprint in some countries is higher (energy use, transport, diet, consumption). Emphasise that countries that contribute least are often those that suffer most from climate change.

teach.heading: Ways to reduce our footprint
bullets: Use public transport, walk or cycle.
Turn off lights and appliances, and insulate homes.
Waste less food and buy less, repair more.
teach.note: Ask pupils to rank actions by impact, from small (turning off lights) to large (reducing flights, home heating, car use). Discuss that individual actions matter but governments and businesses make big decisions. Encourage a positive, solutions-focused tone.

teach.heading: Sustainable development
bullets: Meet needs today without harming the future.
Examples: renewable energy, recycling, fair trade.
teach.note: Introduce the three pillars: social, economic and environmental. Ask pupils to apply them to a new wind farm. Link to khalifah: we hold the Earth in trust for those who come after us.

teach.heading: Assessment overview
bullets: Section A: key terms and short answers.
Section C: a six-mark decision-making question.
teach.note: Remind pupils how to answer a 6-mark question: make a point, give evidence, explain, link to the question. Use command words: describe, explain, evaluate. Tell pupils to use at least two key terms in each answer. Distribute the assessment and set a timer for about 25 minutes.

practice: Calculate the carbon footprint of a school day journey: car 5 km, bus 5 km, walking.
Create a one-sentence definition of sustainable development in your own words.
independent: Complete the end-of-unit assessment: key terms, graph and a 6-mark question.
Write a short reflection: what is the most important thing you learned about resources?
Stretch: evaluate how far individual choices can solve global resource problems.
exit: Give one way to be more sustainable at home.
lessons.homework: Make a family pledge with three actions to be more sustainable and display it at home.
lessons.send: Provide a scaffolded assessment with word banks and sentence starters. EAL: allow bilingual dictionaries. Stretch: add a 9-mark evaluation question on energy choices.

lessons.unit: Spring 1: Earning a living and globalisation
lessons.title: What kind of work do we do in the UK? Economic sectors (3.1)
lessons.bigQuestion: Is a farmer, a factory worker or a software designer more important to the economy?
objectives: To understand how jobs are classified into economic sectors
successCriteria: All: name and define the four economic sectors
Most: classify jobs into sectors
Some: describe the UK's employment structure from a chart
lessons.smsc: Moral: the dignity of honest work

keywords.def: jobs that take raw materials from the earth or sea
jobs that make or build things
jobs that provide services
jobs in research, information and high technology
the share of workers in each sector

hook.text: Think about your breakfast this morning. How many different jobs were needed to get it to your table?

islamicLink.text: Allah says: 'When the prayer has ended, disperse in the land and seek the bounty of Allah' (al-Jumu'ah 62:10). The Prophet, peace be upon him, said that no one eats better food than what he earns by the work of his own hands (Sahih al-Bukhari). Every honest job, in any sector, is valued in Islam.

starter.q: Name a job you would like to do.

teach.heading: Four sectors
teach.note: Follow a loaf of bread: farmer (primary), baker in a factory (secondary), shop worker (tertiary), scientist improving wheat (quaternary).

teach.heading: Classify the jobs
teach.note: Pupils give letters and columns.

teach.heading: The UK today
bullets: Very few work in farming, fishing or mining
teach.note: Figures are rounded and approximate for the 2020s.

teach.heading: Reading the chart
teach.note: Model a description.

steps: Biggest: tertiary and quaternary, about 84%
Then: secondary, about 15%
Smallest: primary, about 1%
Conclude: a service economy
model.answer: Most UK jobs (about 84%) are in services; few are primary (about 1%).

teach.heading: Check
teach.note: Share results.

check.q: A nurse works in which sector?
check.why: Nurses provide a service, so tertiary.

practice.q: Classify: a farmer, a baker in a factory, a delivery driver.
practice.a: Primary, secondary, tertiary
practice.model:
Farmer: takes from nature: primary.
Factory baker: makes things: secondary.
Driver: a service: tertiary.

practice.q: What is the quaternary sector?
practice.a: Research, information and high-technology jobs

practice.q: Roughly what share of UK jobs are in services?
practice.a: About four in five or more (about 84%)

independent.q: Core: Make a four-column table with five jobs in each sector, including jobs in your own family or community.
independent.a: Correct jobs in each sector, for example primary: farmer; secondary: builder; tertiary: imam, teacher; quaternary: researcher
independent.model: Teacher shows it first: 'Tertiary: imam (a service to the community), teacher, nurse.'

independent.q: Extend: In the portal response box, describe the UK's employment structure using the pie chart.
independent.a: Description with figures: services dominant about 84%, secondary about 15%, primary about 1%

independent.q: Stretch: Why might a poorer country have far more primary jobs?
independent.a: More people farm and mine; less industry and fewer services

exit.q: A builder works in the:
exit.a: Secondary sector

exit.q: Big question: is a farmer, a factory worker or a software designer more important to the economy?
exit.a: All are needed and linked; the UK has most jobs in services, but primary and secondary jobs supply the goods

lessons.homework: Ask three adults you know what sector their job is in and why.
lessons.send: SEND: job picture cards to sort. EAL: farm, make, serve, research. Stretch: research one quaternary job in the UK.

lessons.unit: Spring 1: Earning a living and globalisation
lessons.title: The UK's changing employment; change in and around Doncaster (3.2, 3.3)
lessons.bigQuestion: What happens to a town when its main industry closes?
objectives: To understand how UK employment has changed over time, using Doncaster as an example
successCriteria: All: describe how UK employment changed from 1900 to today
Most: describe how Doncaster's jobs changed
Some: explain the effects of deindustrialisation on a community
lessons.crossCurricular: History: the Industrial Revolution and its decline
lessons.smsc: Social: how communities cope with change

keywords.def: the decline of manufacturing and mining
a coal mine and its buildings
storing and moving goods
not having a paid job when you want one
improving a run-down area

hook.text: If the factory where most of your neighbours worked closed tomorrow, what would change in your street?

starter.q: A coal miner works in the:

teach.heading: UK change over time
teach.note: Show the change as a simple before-and-after.

teach.heading: Doncaster: coal and rail
bullets: Surrounded by coal mines in the 1900s
teach.note: Doncaster is in South Yorkshire.

teach.heading: Pits close
teach.note: Effects spread: shops, families and whole villages were hit.

teach.heading: New jobs
teach.note: Doncaster is close to major motorways and railways, which suits logistics.

teach.heading: Check
teach.note: Share results.

options: The decline of mining and manufacturing
check.why: It is the decline of industry, as happened in Doncaster's coalfield.

practice.q: Describe how Doncaster's jobs changed.
practice.a: From coal mining and railway engineering to logistics, retail and services
practice.model:
Past: coal mines and the railway works.
Change: mines closed from the 1980s to 2015.
Now: warehouses, logistics, shops and services.

practice.q: Give one effect of pit closures on a community.
practice.a: For example: unemployment, shops closing, people moving away

practice.q: Why does Doncaster suit logistics?
practice.a: Good motorway and rail links

independent.q: Core: Make a timeline of Doncaster's economy with four stages and one sentence each.
independent.a: 1900s coal and railway works; 1923 and 1938 famous locomotives; 1980s to 2015 pit closures; 2000s onwards logistics and services
